stem: A Driftlight analyst drags the dimension `Plan` onto Color on the Marks card. What does Tableau display?

options.text: A continuous range of colours with a start value and an end value in the legend
options.rationale: This quantitative legend is what a continuous field (typically a measure) gets, not a dimension.

options.text: One colour for every plan, with the opacity of the marks changing by plan
options.rationale: Opacity is a separate formatting setting; a dimension on Color assigns distinct colours.

options.text: A categorical palette, with a distinct colour and a legend entry for each plan
options.rationale: A discrete field on Color gets a categorical palette, one colour per member, plus a legend.

options.text: A single legend entry named Plan, with all the marks in the default blue
options.rationale: Encoding with a field splits the marks by colour; they do not all stay blue.

explanation: Dropping a field on Color encodes it. A discrete field (typically a dimension) gets a categorical palette with one colour per member, and Tableau adds a legend that lists them.

stem: What kind of legend does Tableau show when `AVG(Monthly Price)` is placed on Color?

options.text: A quantitative legend with a continuous range of colours
options.rationale: A continuous field (typically a measure) on Color gets a gradient legend.

options.text: A categorical legend with one swatch for each distinct price
options.rationale: Categorical palettes belong to discrete fields; this aggregated measure is continuous.

options.text: No legend, because a measure can only be used to format all marks equally
options.rationale: Any field on Color is an encoding and creates a legend, whatever its type.

options.text: A stepped legend with ten fixed bins that cannot be changed
options.rationale: Stepped Color is an optional setting in Edit Colors; the default is a continuous range.

explanation: The palette follows the continuity of the field on Color. Discrete fields get distinct colours; continuous fields get a gradient and a quantitative legend.

stem: The analyst wants every mark on a sheet to be orange, with no legend and no change to what the view shows. What should they do?

options.text: Drag `Plan` to Color and assign orange to each member in Edit Colors
options.rationale: This encodes a field, which adds a legend and splits the marks by member.

options.text: Choose Format > Font and set the colour of the pane text to orange
options.rationale: Format > Font changes text in the pane and headers, not the colour of marks.

options.text: Choose Format > Workbook and set a workbook-wide mark colour
options.rationale: The Format Workbook pane sets fonts, not the colour of the marks on a sheet.

options.text: Click Color on the Marks card and pick orange from the menu
options.rationale: Clicking Color without dropping a field formats every mark and adds no legend.

explanation: Clicking Color on the Marks card without dropping a field is formatting: it recolours every mark the same way. Dropping a field is encoding and always creates a legend.

stem: The analyst wants to choose a different palette for the field currently on Color. Which path on the Marks card opens the right dialog?

options.text: Shape > Edit Shape
options.rationale: Edit Shape changes the shapes of marks, not their colours.

options.text: Color > Edit Colors
options.rationale: Edit Colors is where you pick a colour or assign a palette; the colour legend menu offers the same command.

options.text: Size > Edit Sizes
options.rationale: Edit Sizes controls how mark sizes vary, not their colours.

options.text: Label > Edit Colors
options.rationale: Label controls text on the marks; the palette dialog is reached through Color.

explanation: On the Marks card, click Color and then Edit Colors, or use Edit Colors from the colour legend menu. For a discrete field you can pick a colour per member or assign a palette.

stem: A continuous field is on Color. Which Edit Colors setting groups its values into uniform bins instead of a smooth gradient?

options.text: Reversed
options.rationale: Reversed inverts the colours of the palette; it does not create bins.

options.text: Stepped Color
options.rationale: Stepped Color divides the values into uniform bins, each with its own colour.

options.text: Use Full Color Range
options.rationale: This stretches a diverging palette across the full range; it does not bin the values.

options.text: Assign Palette
options.rationale: Assign Palette applies a palette to the members of a discrete field.

explanation: For a continuous field you can choose a sequential or diverging palette. Stepped Color groups the values into uniform bins, and Reversed inverts the colours.

stem: Before the analyst changes anything, how does Tableau draw most marks and the text marks of a new view?

options.text: Most marks in grey, text in black, and all marks with a thin dark border
options.rationale: The default colour of most marks is blue, and by default there is no border.

options.text: Most marks in blue, text in blue, and all marks with a white halo
options.rationale: Text is black by default, and halos only apply with a background image or a map.

options.text: Most marks in orange, text in grey, and all marks without a border
options.rationale: Orange is not the default colour; most marks start out blue and text black.

options.text: Most marks in blue, text in black, and all marks without a border
options.rationale: Blue is the default colour for most marks, black for text, and marks have no border by default.

explanation: Every mark has a default colour: blue for most marks and black for text. By default Tableau draws marks without a border, so borders are a format you switch on.

stem: Which actions encode data on the Marks card and create a legend? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Dragging `Genre` onto Color
options.rationale: A field on Color is an encoding with a categorical palette and a legend.

options.text: Clicking Color and choosing a red from the menu
options.rationale: This formats every mark the same way; no field is involved and no legend appears.

options.text: Dragging `SUM(Minutes Watched)` onto Color
options.rationale: A measure on Color is an encoding too, with a quantitative legend.

options.text: Clicking Color and moving the Opacity slider
options.rationale: Opacity is formatting for all marks and adds no legend.

options.text: Clicking Color and switching on mark borders
options.rationale: Borders are formatting; they do not depend on a field.

explanation: Encoding means dropping a field on Color, which adds information and a legend. Clicking Color without a field only changes how all marks look.

stem: Which statements about colour palettes in Edit Colors are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: A diverging palette can be chosen for a continuous field.
options.rationale: Diverging palettes are offered for continuous fields.

options.text: A discrete field on Color uses a sequential gradient by default.
options.rationale: A discrete field gets a categorical palette with one colour per member.

options.text: Stepped Color is available for a continuous field.
options.rationale: Stepped Color groups the values of a continuous field into uniform bins.

options.text: Use Full Color Range works with every palette of a discrete field.
options.rationale: It applies to a diverging palette on a continuous field, not to discrete members.

options.text: Tableau 10 is an ordinal palette listed at the bottom.
options.rationale: Categorical palettes such as Tableau 10 are at the top; ordinal ones such as Orange are at the bottom.

explanation: The palette follows the continuity of the field. Continuous colour has sequential and diverging palettes plus Stepped Color; discrete colour has categorical palettes.

stem: Which settings can the analyst change after clicking Color on the Marks card, without dropping any field? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Opacity of all marks
options.rationale: The Color menu sets opacity for every mark.

options.text: Stepped Color
options.rationale: Stepped Color needs a continuous field on Color.

options.text: Borders around the marks
options.rationale: By default marks have no border; the Color menu can add one.

options.text: Reversed
options.rationale: Reversing a palette needs a field on Color.

options.text: Assign Palette
options.rationale: Assigning a palette needs the members of a discrete field on Color.

explanation: The Color menu formats every mark: its colour, opacity and borders. The palette options in Edit Colors only make sense once a field is on Color.

stem: Which statements about the default look of marks are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: For most marks, blue is the default colour.
options.rationale: Most marks start out blue.

options.text: Most marks are grey until a field is placed on Color.
options.rationale: The default colour is blue, not grey.

options.text: Text marks are black by default.
options.rationale: Black is the default colour for text.

options.text: Text marks are blue by default.
options.rationale: Blue is the default for most marks, but text is black.

options.text: Marks are drawn with a thin white border by default.
options.rationale: By default Tableau displays all marks without a border.

explanation: Marks start with a default colour: blue for most marks and black for text. Without a border, they only change when you format them or encode a field on Color.

stem: The analyst wants one font for every title, label and header in the whole workbook. Which menu path should they use?

options.text: Format > Workbook
options.rationale: The Format Workbook pane changes all font settings in a workbook.

options.text: Format > Font
options.rationale: Format > Font formats the pane and header text of the current sheet only.

options.text: Format > Borders
options.rationale: Borders are a part of the view to format on one sheet, and not a font setting.

options.text: Format > Animations
options.rationale: Animations control transitions between views, not fonts.

explanation: Format > Workbook opens the Format Workbook pane, where one change reaches all font settings in the workbook, including titles of worksheets, stories and dashboards.

stem: The analyst chooses Format > Workbook. What changes in the Tableau window?

options.text: A dialog opens over the view and blocks the sheet until it is closed
options.rationale: Workbook formatting happens in a pane, not in a modal dialog.

options.text: A new tab named Workbook appears on the Marks card
options.rationale: The Marks card is not involved; the pane sits where the Data pane was.

options.text: The Format Workbook pane replaces the Data pane
options.rationale: The pane takes the place of the Data pane while it is open.

options.text: The Data pane stays and a font list is added below the Filters shelf
options.rationale: The Format Workbook pane replaces the Data pane instead of sitting beside it.

explanation: Opening Format > Workbook shows a pane in place of the Data pane. From there you change all font settings of the workbook, as well as the titles of worksheets, stories and dashboards.

stem: The analyst made a sheet-level change to a header font. Later a colleague changes the font under Format > Workbook. What happens to the sheet-level change?

options.text: It is kept, because sheet-level formatting always wins
options.rationale: Workbook-level font changes overwrite sheet-level ones, not the other way around.

options.text: It is kept for headers but overwritten for pane text
options.rationale: Tableau does not split sheet-level font changes this way; they are overwritten.

options.text: Tableau asks which of the two fonts to keep for every sheet
options.rationale: There is no such prompt; the workbook setting simply takes over.

options.text: It is overwritten by the new workbook font
options.rationale: Changing the workbook font overwrites font changes made at sheet level.

explanation: Workbook formatting is the broadest scope. Applying a font there overwrites font changes made on individual sheets, so set the workbook font first and make exceptions afterwards.

stem: After setting several fonts in the Format Workbook pane, the analyst wants to undo all of it. Which command does that?

options.text: Reset All Sheets
options.rationale: Reset All Sheets belongs to Animations and returns sheets to the workbook default.

options.text: Reset to Defaults
options.rationale: Reset to Defaults in the Format Workbook pane undoes the workbook changes.

options.text: Clear Sheet
options.rationale: Clear Sheet empties the current view; it does not touch workbook formatting.

options.text: Assign Palette
options.rationale: Assign Palette is for colours of a discrete field, not for fonts.

explanation: The Format Workbook pane has a Reset to Defaults command that returns the formatting to Tableau's defaults.

stem: What does Format > Font apply to?

options.text: The pane text or the header text, or both, of the current view
options.rationale: Format > Font works on the view of the current sheet, for either pane or header text.

options.text: Every sheet, dashboard and story title in the workbook
options.rationale: That is the reach of Format > Workbook, not of Format > Font.

options.text: Only the text on the Marks card Label property
options.rationale: Format > Font formats the pane and header text of the view, not only labels.

options.text: Only the titles of stories and dashboards
options.rationale: Titles of stories and dashboards are handled in the Format Workbook pane.

explanation: Format > Font is sheet-level formatting. For one view you can set the font, style, size and colour of the pane text, the header text or both.

stem: The head of design wants a consistent look in a workbook, with a few exceptions on individual sheets. What is the best order of work?

options.text: Format each sheet first, then apply the font under Format > Workbook
options.rationale: The workbook font would overwrite every sheet-level change made earlier.

options.text: Use Format > Workbook for the exceptions and Format > Font for the baseline
options.rationale: This reverses the scopes: workbook is broad and sheet-level is specific.

options.text: Set the workbook font first, then override the exceptions on those sheets
options.rationale: The workbook setting is the baseline; later sheet-level changes stay.

options.text: Set a font on every sheet separately and never open Format > Workbook
options.rationale: This works but is slow, and misses titles of stories and dashboards that the workbook pane covers.

explanation: Start broad, then refine. The workbook font gives every sheet the same base look, and the sheet-level exceptions come after it so they are not overwritten.

stem: Which items can be changed in the Format Workbook pane? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: All font settings in the workbook
options.rationale: The pane changes all font settings in a workbook.

options.text: The join type between two tables
options.rationale: Joins are set in the data source, not in the Format pane.

options.text: The font settings for titles of worksheets, stories and dashboards
options.rationale: Titles of these are covered by the Format Workbook pane.

options.text: The data type of every dimension
options.rationale: Data types are changed in the Data pane or data source, not by formatting.

options.text: The default aggregation of every measure
options.rationale: Default properties are not set in the Format Workbook pane.

explanation: The Format Workbook pane is for appearance: all fonts in the workbook, plus the titles of worksheets, stories and dashboards.

stem: For a view formatted with Format > Font, which properties can the analyst specify for pane text or header text? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: The font
options.rationale: Font is one of the properties you can specify.

options.text: The sort order of the members
options.rationale: Sorting is not a font property.

options.text: The size
options.rationale: Size is one of the properties you can specify.

options.text: The data source connection
options.rationale: Connections are not part of text formatting.

options.text: The colour
options.rationale: Colour is one of the properties you can specify.

options.text: The aggregation of the measure
options.rationale: Aggregation is a pill setting, not a font property.

explanation: For a view you can set font, style, size and colour for the pane text, the header text or both.

stem: Which statements about workbook-level and sheet-level fonts are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Format > Workbook can overwrite font changes made on individual sheets.
options.rationale: The workbook setting takes over, including sheet-level changes.

options.text: Format > Font changes the font of every sheet in the workbook.
options.rationale: Format > Font only reaches the current sheet.

options.text: Format > Font changes only the pane and header text of the current sheet.
options.rationale: It works at the worksheet level.

options.text: Format > Workbook only works on dashboards.
options.rationale: It covers all font settings in the workbook, sheets included.

options.text: Reset to Defaults only works for one sheet at a time.
options.rationale: It belongs to the Format Workbook pane and resets workbook formatting.

explanation: Workbook is the broad scope and the worksheet is the narrow one. A workbook change reaches every sheet and can overwrite sheet-level fonts; Format > Font stays on one sheet.

stem: Which mark type must be selected on the Marks card for the shapes assigned to a field to show?

options.text: Circle
options.rationale: Circle marks are drawn as circles whatever is on the Shape property.

options.text: Square
options.rationale: Square marks are drawn as squares and ignore the shapes.

options.text: Shape
options.rationale: Shapes only appear when the mark type is Shape.

options.text: Text
options.rationale: Text marks show words; they do not draw shapes.

explanation: Set the mark type to Shape, then drag a field to Shape on the Marks card. Tableau then draws a different shape for each member.

stem: What does Tableau do when the dimension `Device` is placed on Shape?

options.text: It separates the marks by member and assigns a unique shape to each
options.rationale: A dimension on Shape splits the marks by member, with a shape per member.

options.text: It converts `Device` to a measure and uses one shape for all marks
options.rationale: Only a measure is converted (to a discrete measure); a dimension is kept.

options.text: It keeps one mark per row and varies only the size of the shapes
options.rationale: Size is a separate property; Shape assigns a different shape per member.

options.text: It uses one shape but adds a legend with the names of the members
options.rationale: Each member gets its own shape, which is what the legend shows.

explanation: Placing a dimension on Shape splits the marks according to its members and gives each member a shape. The legend lists which shape stands for which member.

stem: Which view makes the Automatic mark type pick Shape?

options.text: A continuous date on Columns and a measure on Rows
options.rationale: This combination is drawn as a line.

options.text: A measure as the innermost field on Rows and another measure on Columns
options.rationale: Automatic uses Shape when measures are the innermost fields on both shelves.

options.text: A dimension on Columns and a measure on Rows
options.rationale: A dimension with a measure is drawn as bars.

options.text: A dimension on Columns and another dimension on Rows
options.rationale: Only dimensions with no continuous field gives text.

explanation: When measures are the innermost fields on both Rows and Columns, Automatic picks the Shape mark. You can also set the mark type to Shape yourself.

stem: A dimension with 14 members is placed on Shape and the default shapes are used. What happens?

options.text: Tableau shows a message and refuses to draw more than ten members
options.rationale: There is no such limit on members; the default shapes repeat.

options.text: The extra four members are drawn as plain circles without a shape
options.rationale: The shapes repeat; the remaining members do not turn into circles.

options.text: The four smallest members are grouped into one member called Other
options.rationale: Tableau does not group members automatically.

options.text: Ten unique shapes are used, and the shapes repeat for the remaining members
options.rationale: By default, ten unique shapes are used to encode dimensions, then they repeat.

explanation: The default shape palette has ten shapes. With more than ten members they repeat, so two members can share a shape; assign shapes by hand or filter to avoid that.

stem: Which command on the shape legend's card menu opens the dialog for choosing other shapes?

options.text: Edit Shape
options.rationale: Edit Shape (or clicking Shape on the Marks card) lets you pick shapes from palettes.

options.text: Edit Colors
options.rationale: Edit Colors changes the palette of the Color property.

options.text: Edit Sizes
options.rationale: Edit Sizes changes how sizes vary on the Size property.

options.text: Reload Shapes
options.rationale: Reload Shapes refreshes the custom shape palettes from the repository after a change.

explanation: You can click Shape on the Marks card, or use Edit Shape on the legend's menu. There you choose from palettes such as filled shapes, arrows and weather symbols.

stem: The analyst has a set of PNG image files that should become a custom shape palette. Where do they go?

options.text: In a new folder inside My Tableau Repository\Datasources
options.rationale: Datasources holds connection files, not shape palettes.

options.text: In a new folder inside My Tableau Repository\Workbooks
options.rationale: Workbooks holds workbook files; Tableau reads shapes from the Shapes folder.

options.text: In a new folder inside My Tableau Repository\Shapes
options.rationale: The folder name becomes the name of the palette.

options.text: In the same folder as the workbook that will use them
options.rationale: Tableau reads custom shapes from the repository, not from beside the workbook.

explanation: Copy the image files into a new folder in My Tableau Repository\Shapes. The folder name becomes the palette name and shows up in the Edit Shape dialog.

stem: Tableau was running when the analyst copied a new folder of images into the Shapes folder. The palette is missing in Edit Shape. What should they do?

options.text: Click Assign Palette in the Edit Colors dialog
options.rationale: Assign Palette is about colour, not shapes.

options.text: Click Reload Shapes in the Edit Shape dialog
options.rationale: Reload Shapes loads the new palette without restarting.

options.text: Choose Data > Refresh All Extracts
options.rationale: Extract refreshes update data, not shape palettes.

options.text: Drag a measure onto Shape on the Marks card
options.rationale: This would convert the measure to discrete but not load new images.

explanation: If Tableau was already running, use Reload Shapes in the Edit Shape dialog so that the new palette appears.

stem: Which image file formats can be used for custom shapes? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: .gif
options.rationale: GIF is listed as supported.

options.text: .xlsx
options.rationale: A spreadsheet is not an image format.

options.text: .bmp
options.rationale: BMP is listed as supported.

options.text: .pdf
options.rationale: PDF is not among the formats for custom shapes.

options.text: .tiff
options.rationale: TIFF is listed as supported.

options.text: .csv
options.rationale: A text data file is not an image.

explanation: Custom shapes are image files: .png, .gif, .jpg, .bmp or .tiff, copied into a folder in My Tableau Repository\Shapes.

stem: Which statements about fields on Shape are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: A dimension on Shape gets a unique shape per member.
options.rationale: Marks are separated by the members of the dimension.

options.text: A measure on Shape stays continuous and gets a gradient.
options.rationale: A measure on Shape is converted to a discrete measure.

options.text: A measure on Shape is converted to a discrete measure.
options.rationale: Shape needs discrete values, so the measure is converted.

options.text: A dimension on Shape adds no legend.
options.rationale: A field on Shape is an encoding and adds a legend.

options.text: Shapes never repeat, however many members there are.
options.rationale: By default ten shapes are used and they repeat after that.

explanation: Shape is a discrete encoding: dimensions get one shape per member, and a measure is turned into a discrete measure first.

stem: The analyst wants marks to move smoothly on every sheet of the workbook when a filter changes. Where do they turn this on?

options.text: Format > Animations, then On under Workbook Default
options.rationale: The Workbook Default setting applies animation to every sheet.

options.text: Format > Workbook, then a switch in the Format Workbook pane
options.rationale: That pane holds font settings for the whole workbook, not animation.

options.text: The Marks card, by clicking Size and choosing a transition
options.rationale: Size controls how big marks are; animation is not a Marks card property.

options.text: Format > Font, then a transition option for pane text
options.rationale: Format > Font sets font, style, size and color of text, not animation.

explanation: Animations are configured under Format > Animations. The Workbook Default section turns them on for all sheets, and Selected Sheet overrides it for one.

stem: What is the longest custom duration that can be set for a viz animation?

options.text: 1 second
options.rationale: Presets are short, but a custom duration can be longer than this.

options.text: 30 seconds
options.rationale: This is more than the limit Tableau allows.

options.text: 10 seconds
options.rationale: A custom duration can be up to 10 seconds; presets are also available.

options.text: 60 seconds
options.rationale: This is far beyond the allowed maximum.

explanation: Under Format > Animations, Duration offers a preset or a custom duration of up to 10 seconds.

stem: The analyst sets the animation Style to Sequential. What does Tableau do when the view changes?

options.text: It plays all the animations at the same time
options.rationale: This describes Simultaneous, which is faster but harder to follow.

options.text: It fades out marks, moves and sorts them, then fades them in
options.rationale: This is the Sequential style: one step after another, easier to follow.

options.text: It animates only the sheet that is currently selected
options.rationale: Which sheets animate depends on Workbook Default and Selected Sheet, not on Style.

options.text: It holds each mark on screen for the full 10 seconds
options.rationale: Duration is a separate setting; Style controls the order of the steps.

explanation: Style has two choices. Simultaneous plays every animation at once and is faster; Sequential fades out marks, moves and sorts them, then fades them in, which is easier to follow.

stem: Animations are on for the whole workbook, but one dashboard sheet should use the Sequential style. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Change the Style under Workbook Default
options.rationale: This would change the style of every sheet, not just one.

options.text: Click Reset All Sheets
options.rationale: This returns every sheet to the workbook default, so the exception would be lost.

options.text: Use Format > Workbook and pick a different title font
options.rationale: Fonts have nothing to do with how marks animate.

options.text: Change the settings under Selected Sheet
options.rationale: Selected Sheet overrides the workbook defaults for that one sheet.

explanation: Workbook Default sets the animation for all sheets. To deviate on a particular sheet, change the settings under Selected Sheet.

stem: Several sheets have their own animation overrides, and the analyst wants all of them to follow the workbook default again. Which command does that?

options.text: Reset to Defaults in the Format Workbook pane
options.rationale: That command undoes font changes made in the Format Workbook pane, not animation overrides.

options.text: Turning Selected Sheet off on each sheet in turn
options.rationale: This is slower and not how the overrides are cleared in one step.

options.text: Reset All Sheets
options.rationale: It returns every sheet to the workbook default.

options.text: Setting the duration to 0 seconds
options.rationale: A different duration is still an override, and it does not restore the default.

explanation: Format > Animations includes Reset All Sheets, which removes the per-sheet overrides so each sheet uses the workbook default.

stem: What is the purpose of animating a viz?

options.text: Marks move smoothly when filters, sorts or the view change, so viewers can follow what happened
options.rationale: Smooth transitions help viewers track the change.

options.text: Each mark gets a legend entry that updates when the data changes
options.rationale: Legends come from fields on Color, Size and Shape, not from animation.

options.text: The data is refreshed automatically at set intervals
options.rationale: Animation changes how a change is shown, not when data updates.

options.text: The view shrinks so that more marks fit in the pane
options.rationale: Animation does not change the size of the view.

explanation: Animations show a change as motion instead of a jump. A viewer can follow where marks went after a filter, a sort or a change to the view.

stem: Which statements about the animation Style are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Simultaneous plays all the animations at once
options.rationale: This is the definition of Simultaneous, and it is the faster style.

options.text: Sequential plays all the animations at once
options.rationale: Sequential is the step-by-step style; Simultaneous plays everything at once.

options.text: Sequential fades out marks, moves and sorts them, then fades them in
options.rationale: That is the Sequential order, which is easier to follow.

options.text: The Style can only be chosen once per workbook
options.rationale: Selected Sheet lets a single sheet override the workbook default.

options.text: Simultaneous gives each mark its own legend while it moves
options.rationale: Style does not affect legends.

explanation: Style chooses between two ways of playing a transition. Simultaneous is faster; Sequential steps through fade out, move and sort, and fade in.

stem: Which settings can be chosen under Format > Animations? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: A Duration, either a preset or a custom value
options.rationale: Duration is one of the animation settings.

options.text: The font of the pane text
options.rationale: Fonts are set under Format > Font or Format > Workbook.

options.text: A Style, Simultaneous or Sequential
options.rationale: Style is the second animation setting.

options.text: The categorical palette for Color
options.rationale: Palettes belong to Color on the Marks card, under Edit Colors.

options.text: The width of fixed-width bars
options.rationale: Fixed bar width is set after clicking Size on the Marks card.

explanation: Format > Animations holds a workbook default (on or off), the duration, the style and the Selected Sheet overrides. Colours, fonts and sizes are formatted elsewhere.

stem: Animations are on with the Simultaneous style for the workbook. The head of design wants the `Engagement` sheet to use Sequential, and every other sheet to stay as it is. Which steps achieve this? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Open Format > Animations
options.rationale: All animation settings, including sheet overrides, are on this menu path.

options.text: Change the Style under Workbook Default
options.rationale: This would switch every sheet to Sequential.

options.text: With the sheet selected, change the Style under Selected Sheet
options.rationale: The override applies to that sheet only.

options.text: Click Reset All Sheets
options.rationale: This removes overrides rather than creating one.

options.text: Change the workbook font under Format > Workbook
options.rationale: Fonts do not affect the animation style.

explanation: Per-sheet exceptions are set under Selected Sheet in the Animations pane. The workbook default stays untouched, so the other sheets keep Simultaneous.

stem: The analyst wants every mark on a sheet to be larger, without adding a field. What should they do?

options.text: Drag `Minutes Watched` onto Size on the Marks card
options.rationale: A field on Size encodes data, so marks would differ in size by value.

options.text: Click Size on the Marks card and move the slider to the right
options.rationale: The slider sets the size of all marks at once.

options.text: Choose Format > Workbook and increase the font size
options.rationale: Fonts affect text, not marks.

options.text: Use Edit Sizes in the Color legend menu
options.rationale: Edit Sizes belongs to a size legend, which only exists once a field is on Size.

explanation: Clicking Size without a field formats all marks the same. Moving the slider changes their size, with no legend and no change to the data.

stem: After the analyst moves the Size slider on the Marks card, what has changed?

options.text: The data view is resized, and the marks keep their size
options.rationale: It is the other way round: the view stays the same.

options.text: The values of the measures are scaled up or down
options.rationale: Size is a visual property and never changes the data.

options.text: Each dimension member gets its own unique size
options.rationale: That happens when a discrete field is placed on Size, not with the slider.

options.text: The marks are drawn larger or smaller, but the size of the data view is not modified
options.rationale: The slider only affects the marks.

explanation: The slider is formatting. It changes how big the marks are drawn, and Tableau states that the size of the data view is not modified.

stem: A continuous measure such as `AVG(Runtime)` is placed on Size. How does Tableau assign mark sizes?

options.text: The smallest value gets the smallest mark and the largest value the largest mark
options.rationale: This is how a continuous field is encoded on Size.

options.text: Every mark gets the same size, as the field only adds a legend
options.rationale: A field on Size changes the marks; it is not a legend-only change.

options.text: The marks are sorted by value, and sizes alternate small and large
options.rationale: Sizes follow the value, not an alternation.

options.text: The largest value gets the smallest mark, unless Reversed is cleared
options.rationale: Reversed is an option in Edit Sizes; by default, bigger values get bigger marks.

explanation: A continuous field on Size maps the range of values to the range of mark sizes. Edit Sizes can reverse this.

stem: A discrete field is placed on Size. What does Tableau do?

options.text: It gives all members the largest size
options.rationale: Members are told apart by size, so they cannot all be the same.

options.text: It converts the field to a measure and sums it
options.rationale: Placing a field on Size does not aggregate a dimension that way.

options.text: It assigns a unique size to each member
options.rationale: Discrete members each get their own size.

options.text: It ignores the field until the mark type is Shape
options.rationale: Size works with any mark type; the Shape requirement belongs to Shape.

explanation: The encoding follows the field's continuity: a continuous field maps its range to a range of sizes, and a discrete field gets a unique size per member.

stem: From which place does the analyst open Edit Sizes, to choose Automatic, By range or From zero?

options.text: The Format > Workbook pane
options.rationale: This pane sets fonts for the workbook.

options.text: The Format > Animations pane
options.rationale: That pane sets transitions between views, not how values map to mark sizes.

options.text: The Data pane, by right-clicking the field
options.rationale: The field's menu in the Data pane doesn't hold size ranges.

options.text: The menu of the size legend
options.rationale: Edit Sizes is on the size legend's menu.

explanation: Each legend has a card menu with its own editing command: Edit Colors, Edit Shape or Edit Sizes. The size legend offers Edit Sizes.

stem: The bars of a chart on a continuous date axis should all have the same fixed width. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Drag the date field to Size on the Marks card
options.rationale: This would encode the date in the mark size instead of fixing it.

options.text: Click Size, choose Fixed, then enter the Width in axis units
options.rationale: On a continuous date axis, the width is entered in days.

options.text: Move the Size slider to the far right
options.rationale: The slider changes the size of all marks but doesn't set a width in axis units.

options.text: Set the Style to Simultaneous under Format > Animations
options.rationale: Style is an animation setting and has no effect on bar width.

explanation: Size has a Fixed option with a Width in axis units. When the axis is a continuous date axis, the unit is days.

stem: Which statements about Edit Sizes are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Reversed gives the biggest mark to the smallest value
options.rationale: Reversed flips the default assignment of sizes.

options.text: Edit Sizes opens from the Format menu
options.rationale: It opens from the size legend's menu.

options.text: Sizes can only vary Automatically
options.rationale: They can also vary By range or From zero.

options.text: The start and end values can be fixed
options.rationale: The range can be pinned instead of following the data.

options.text: Edit Sizes is only available for text marks
options.rationale: It belongs to the size legend of a field on Size, not to one mark type.

explanation: Edit Sizes on the size legend controls how values map to mark sizes: Automatically, By range or From zero, optionally reversed, with fixed start and end values.

stem: Which actions change the size of marks? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Clicking Size on the Marks card and moving the slider
options.rationale: This sets the size of all marks.

options.text: Clicking Color and moving the Opacity slider
options.rationale: Opacity changes transparency, not size.

options.text: Dragging a field onto Size on the Marks card
options.rationale: The field's values decide each mark's size.

options.text: Choosing Format > Font and a larger pane font
options.rationale: This enlarges text, not marks.

options.text: Setting the Duration under Format > Animations
options.rationale: Duration only controls how long a transition lasts.

explanation: There are two ways to size marks: format all of them with the slider, or encode with a field on Size.

stem: Which statements about a field on Size are true? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: With a continuous field, the smallest value gets the smallest mark
options.rationale: The range of values maps to the range of sizes.

options.text: The size legend, once the field is placed, lets the analyst open Edit Sizes
options.rationale: The legend's menu holds the editing command.

options.text: A discrete field gets a unique size for each member
options.rationale: Each member is told apart by size.

options.text: The field changes the size of the data view
options.rationale: Only the marks are affected; the view is not resized.

options.text: The field can only be a dimension
options.rationale: Continuous fields, typically measures, work on Size and are the usual choice.

explanation: A field on Size encodes data: a continuous field maps its range of values to a range of mark sizes, a discrete field gives each member its own size, and a legend appears.

stem: When does Tableau display a legend on a sheet?

options.text: Whenever the mark type is changed from Automatic
options.rationale: Changing the mark type does not by itself encode a field.

options.text: Whenever the analyst formats a font under Format > Font
options.rationale: Fonts are formatting and need no key.

options.text: When fields are added to Color, Size or Shape on the Marks card
options.rationale: A legend explains how the view is encoded.

options.text: Whenever a filter is added to the Filters shelf
options.rationale: A filter limits the data; it does not encode a mark property.

explanation: Tableau shows a legend to indicate how the view is encoded. Fields on Color, Size and Shape produce one.

stem: The analyst clicks Color on the Marks card and picks a green for all marks. Which legend appears?

options.text: None, because there is no field to explain
options.rationale: Formatting without a field creates no legend.

options.text: A categorical legend with one green entry
options.rationale: Categorical legends come from a discrete field on Color.

options.text: A quantitative legend with a range of greens
options.rationale: Quantitative legends come from a continuous field on Color.

options.text: A size legend with one entry
options.rationale: A size legend needs a field on Size.

explanation: A legend is created by encoding. Choosing one colour for every mark is only formatting, so there is nothing to explain.

stem: A bar chart already shows every `Genre` name as a label on its bars, and `Genre` is also on Color. Why might the analyst hide the legend?

options.text: A legend can only be hidden once the field is removed from Color
options.rationale: Hiding the card and removing the field are independent actions.

options.text: The legend would otherwise stop the bars from using a categorical palette
options.rationale: Showing a legend never changes the palette.

options.text: Tableau permits only one visible legend per workbook
options.rationale: There is no such limit; each legend is a card on its sheet.

options.text: The marks are already labelled, so the legend repeats what the labels say
options.rationale: A legend can be hidden when the encoding is obvious.

explanation: Legends are cards on the sheet. When the marks are labelled, readers do not need a key, so the legend can be hidden to save space.

stem: Where does the analyst find Edit Colors for a field that is on Color, apart from the Marks card button?

options.text: In the Format > Workbook pane
options.rationale: This pane is for fonts, not palettes.

options.text: In the menu of the color legend card
options.rationale: Each legend card has its own menu, which holds Edit Colors.

options.text: In the Filters card of the sheet
options.rationale: Filter cards have their own menus; palettes are not edited there.

options.text: In the Format > Animations pane, under Selected Sheet
options.rationale: Animations settings control transitions, not palettes.

explanation: A legend is a card, and its menu holds the matching edit command: Edit Colors, Edit Shape or Edit Sizes.

stem: Which of these sheets most needs its legend kept visible?

options.text: A line chart with `Plan` on Color where the lines are not labelled
options.rationale: Readers need the key to know which colour is which plan.

options.text: A bar chart where every bar carries its own name as a label
options.rationale: The labels already tell the reader what each mark is.

options.text: A view in which no field is on Color, Size or Shape
options.rationale: There is no encoding, so no legend to show.

options.text: A sheet whose marks are all coloured orange through the Color menu
options.rationale: One colour for all marks encodes nothing.

explanation: A legend explains an encoding. Hide it where the marks are already labelled or nothing is encoded; keep it where colour is the only way to tell the marks apart.

stem: What kind of element on the sheet is a legend?

options.text: A pill on the Columns shelf
options.rationale: Pills represent fields on shelves; a legend is not one.

options.text: A mark type on the Marks card
options.rationale: Mark types are choices like Bar or Circle.

options.text: A card with its own menu
options.rationale: Legends, like filters, are cards that can be shown or hidden.

options.text: A sheet-level font setting
options.rationale: Fonts are formatted under the Format menu.

explanation: A legend is a card. It can be hidden or shown, and its own menu offers Edit Colors, Edit Shape or Edit Sizes.

stem: Which actions create a legend? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: Dragging `Plan` onto Color
options.rationale: A field on Color is encoded and explained by a legend.

options.text: Clicking Size and moving the slider
options.rationale: This formats all marks without a field.

options.text: Dragging `Type` onto Shape
options.rationale: A field on Shape needs a shape legend.

options.text: Clicking Color and choosing one colour
options.rationale: A single colour for all marks has nothing to explain.

options.text: Dragging `AVG(Runtime)` onto Size
options.rationale: A field on Size gets a size legend.

explanation: Legends appear for fields added to Color, Size and Shape. Formatting marks without a field creates none.

stem: Which statements about legends are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: A legend can be hidden when the marks are already labelled
options.rationale: The encoding is obvious, so the key can go.

options.text: Hiding a legend removes its field from the Marks card
options.rationale: The field stays on the Marks card; only the legend card changes.

options.text: Each legend card has its own menu
options.rationale: That menu also holds Edit Colors, Edit Shape or Edit Sizes.

options.text: A legend must stay visible whenever a field is on Color
options.rationale: It can be hidden and shown again as readers need.

options.text: The legend of a field on Shape shows ten unique shapes at most
options.rationale: That is about the default shapes repeating; it doesn't say how legends are hidden.

explanation: A legend is a card on the sheet. It can be hidden when it's redundant and shown again, and its menu holds the edit command for the encoding.

stem: Which settings create no legend? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Clicking Color and choosing an orange for every mark
options.rationale: There is no field, so nothing to explain.

options.text: Dragging `Genre` onto Color
options.rationale: A discrete field on Color produces a categorical legend.

options.text: Clicking Size and moving the slider
options.rationale: It resizes all marks equally and encodes nothing.

options.text: Dragging `Device` onto Shape
options.rationale: A field on Shape produces a shape legend.

options.text: Dragging `Monthly Price` onto Size
options.rationale: A field on Size produces a size legend.

explanation: A legend explains an encoding. When the Marks card is formatted without a field, every mark looks the same and no legend is needed.

stem: The chart has the dimension `Plan` on Color. How does Tableau tell the viewer which colour belongs to which plan?

options.text: A quantitative legend shows one gradient bar that runs from the smallest plan total to the largest.
options.rationale: A gradient legend belongs to a continuous field on Color. `Plan` is discrete.

options.text: A categorical legend lists each plan with its own distinct colour, and the palette assigns them by member.
options.rationale: A discrete field on Color gets a categorical palette, one colour and one legend entry per member.

options.text: No legend appears, because every bar is already drawn in the default colour of the Marks card.
options.rationale: Dropping a field on Color is encoding, so a legend is created to explain it.

options.text: A stepped legend groups the plans into a few uniform bins and colours each bin.
options.rationale: Stepped Color is an option for continuous colour and bins values. Plans are separate members.

explanation: A discrete field such as a dimension on Color gets a categorical palette. Each member gets a distinct colour, and the legend lists them so the viewer can match a colour to a plan.

stem: On this sheet, `AVG(Monthly Price)` sits on Color, and its pill is blue instead of green. What does that mean for the colours?

options.text: Tableau draws a smooth gradient anyway, because a measure always gets a continuous range of colours.
options.rationale: The palette follows how the pill is treated. A blue pill is discrete, so there is no continuous gradient.

options.text: Tableau shows a diverging palette centred on zero, because the aggregate is an average.
options.rationale: Diverging is a choice of continuous palette. An average does not trigger it, and this pill is discrete.

options.text: Tableau colours every mark the same, because only dimensions can create different colours.
options.rationale: A discrete measure can encode colour. It is simply handled like a discrete field.

options.text: Tableau treats each distinct value as a member, with a categorical palette and one legend entry per value.
options.rationale: A discrete pill on Color gets a categorical palette, even when the field is a measure.

explanation: Continuity, not the field type, decides the legend. A discrete (blue) pill on Color gets a categorical palette with one entry per value. The same measure made continuous (green) gets a quantitative gradient.

stem: The filled map colours each country by `AVG(Monthly Price)`, a continuous field. Which statements about its colours are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The legend is a quantitative legend showing a continuous range of colours from the lowest to the highest value.
options.rationale: A continuous field on Color produces a gradient legend.

options.text: Each country gets its own distinct colour from a categorical palette such as Tableau 10.
options.rationale: Categorical palettes are for discrete fields, where each member gets a colour.

options.text: Edit Colors lets the analyst select one country at a time and assign it a colour by hand.
options.rationale: Picking a colour per member is for discrete fields. A continuous field is edited as a range.

options.text: Edit Colors offers Stepped Color, which groups the values into uniform bins instead of a smooth range.
options.rationale: Stepped Color is an option for continuous colour.

options.text: Moving the Size slider on the Marks card is what switches the legend from categorical to gradient.
options.rationale: Size formats mark size. The legend type follows the field on Color.

explanation: A continuous field on Color shows a gradient, and Edit Colors then works on the range: sequential or diverging palettes, Stepped Color, Reversed. Per-member colours and categorical palettes belong to discrete fields.

stem: Each mark in this scatterplot is a Genre. What does one shape stand for?

options.text: One member of `Type`, so all marks with the same shape share the same `Type`.
options.rationale: The Shape shelf holds `Type`, and each member of a dimension on Shape gets its own shape.

options.text: One `Genre`, so the chart uses a different shape for every genre on the view.
options.rationale: `Genre` is on Detail. It sets how many marks there are, not what the shapes mean.

options.text: One band of `AVG(Runtime)`, so marks with a similar runtime share a shape.
options.rationale: Shapes do not bin a measure. The runtime sets only the vertical position.

options.text: One range of `Titles (Count)`, so marks further right get a different shape.
options.rationale: The count sets the horizontal position. Shapes come from the field on Shape.

explanation: A dimension on Shape splits the marks by its members and assigns a unique shape to each. Detail only decides how many marks there are, and position comes from the axes.

stem: In this scatterplot, the Shape mark type is set and `Device` is on Shape with `Genre` on Detail. What does one mark show?

options.text: All the sessions of one genre, because Shape on its own does not split the marks.
options.rationale: A dimension on Shape does split the marks, just as Detail does.

options.text: All the sessions of one device, because Detail is only used for text labels.
options.rationale: Detail adds a dimension to the level of detail. It is not limited to labels.

options.text: The sessions for one combination of `Genre` and `Device`, drawn with the shape of that device.
options.rationale: Both Detail and Shape dimensions set the level of detail, so there is one mark per combination.

options.text: A single value for the whole sheet, because two aggregated measures on the axes collapse the view.
options.rationale: The dimensions in the view keep the marks apart, so the measures are aggregated per combination.

explanation: Every dimension in the view sets the level of detail, including one on Shape. Here each mark is a unique Genre and Device combination, and its shape tells the viewer which device it is.

stem: Each mark in the chart is a `Genre`, drawn as a circle. The analyst wants Movie and Series titles to have different symbols while keeping one mark per genre. What should they do?

options.text: Drag `Type` to Detail on the Marks card, which gives each member its own symbol.
options.rationale: Detail splits the marks but never changes the symbol. It keeps the circle.

options.text: Drag `Type` to Shape while the mark type stays Circle, because shapes show on every mark type.
options.rationale: Shapes only show when the mark type is Shape. With Circle the marks stay circles.

options.text: Set the mark type to Shape and drag `Type` to Size, so each member gets its own symbol.
options.rationale: Size changes how big marks are. The symbol comes from the field on Shape.

options.text: Set the mark type to Shape and drag `Type` to Shape on the Marks card.
options.rationale: Both steps are needed: the Shape mark type, and a dimension on Shape that assigns one shape per member.

explanation: The Shape card only takes effect with the Shape mark type. Pairing it with a dimension such as `Type` gives each member its own symbol, while `Genre` on Detail still keeps one mark per genre.

stem: In the symbol map, `Subscribers (Count)` is on Size with `City` on Detail. What does a larger circle mean?

options.text: The city has more subscribers than the cities with smaller circles.
options.rationale: A continuous measure on Size gives the largest mark to the largest value.

options.text: The city covers a larger geographic area on the map.
options.rationale: Circle size comes from the field on Size, not from geography.

options.text: The city lies further from the centre of the map.
options.rationale: Position comes from latitude and longitude. Size is a separate encoding.

options.text: The city was added to the data more recently than the other cities.
options.rationale: Nothing on the Marks card refers to dates. Size shows the measure.

explanation: A continuous measure on Size is scaled from the smallest mark for the smallest value to the largest mark for the largest. A bigger circle therefore means a bigger count of subscribers.

stem: The scatterplot has one circle per `Genre`, with `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Size. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A genre drawn higher up has the larger circle, because height decides size.
options.rationale: Height shows `AVG(Minutes Watched)`. Size is its own encoding.

options.text: A larger circle means a larger `SUM(Minutes Watched)`, wherever the genre sits on the axes.
options.rationale: The measure on Size sets the circle size, independently of position.

options.text: A larger circle means more sessions, because Tableau sizes marks by their row count.
options.rationale: Only the measure on Size is used. `Sessions (Count)` sets position on the horizontal axis.

options.text: All the circles have the same size, because a dimension on Detail fixes the size of its marks.
options.rationale: Detail does not fix sizes. The measure on Size varies them.

explanation: A measure on Size adds a third quantity to a two-axis scatterplot. Position still reads from the axes, while circle size reads the Size field, here the total minutes watched.

stem: In this view, which pills produce a legend on the sheet? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: `Plan` on Color
options.rationale: A field on Color is encoded, so a legend explains it.

options.text: `Device` on Shape
options.rationale: A field on Shape is encoded, so a legend lists its shapes.

options.text: `Genre` on Detail
options.rationale: Detail adds marks but encodes nothing visible, so it has no legend.

options.text: `Country` on Tooltip
options.rationale: A tooltip shows a value on hover. It does not create a legend.

options.text: `Sessions (Count)` on Columns
options.rationale: A field on a shelf gets an axis, not a legend.

options.text: `AVG(Minutes Watched)` on Rows
options.rationale: A field on a shelf gets an axis, not a legend.

explanation: Legends appear for fields on Color, Size and Shape, which encode data in the marks. Detail and Tooltip add marks or hover text, and Columns and Rows produce axes or headers.
